description: A timeline comparison of what happened to EV battery prices as the industry scaled—pinching margins, forcing plant delays, and rewarding companies that locked in supply. This race charts the sharp global decline in lithium-ion battery pack prices while a handful of leading cell makers and automakers rode the wave (or paid for misreads).
youtube_description:
🚨 Battery prices didn’t just fall—they detonated. This chart-race visualization tells the story of how EV cell makers surged while the market ruthlessly re-priced the future.

Chapters:
0:00 — 2005–2010: Early scale-up, expensive packs dominate
0:55 — 2011–2014: Gigafactories arrive; $/kWh starts the long slide
2:00 — 2015–2017: Model S/X + growing demand; premium volumes explode
3:00 — 2018–2019: Oversupply fears; chemistry transitions accelerate
4:10 — 2020: EV demand snaps back; supply chains re-tighten
5:05 — 2021: Price war becomes inevitable—scale rewards the winners
6:10 — 2022–2023: Cost shock + rebalancing; margins swing
7:20 — 2024–2025: The survivors lock in cost leadership
9:00 — 2025: Who grew through the crash? CATL and leading automakers.

What you’re seeing: a timeline comparison using revenue proxies for major cell/EV players during the real-world battery price compression era.

Hashtags: #ev #battery #lithiumion #catl #lges #panasonic #tesla #evcharging #energystorage #economics
instagram_caption:
🚀 The $100B EV Battery Crash—who actually won?

For most of the 2010s, EV batteries were the bottleneck and the headline: every investor asked the same question—will battery prices fall fast enough to make electric cars unstoppable? Then the industry did what it always does when the math gets brutal: it scaled. By 2015–2017, cell makers were racing toward gigafactories, longer-term supply deals, and chemistry optimization. The result wasn’t just cheaper packs—it was a brutal reshuffling of the leaderboard.

At the start of this timeline (2005–2010), companies we now associate with dominance were tiny or not yet meaningfully public in this category. But by 2016, the real “turn” shows up: CATL-like growth accelerates sharply (from ~${8.40}B proxy in 2016 to ~${18.20}B by 2018). Meanwhile, Tesla’s battery-driven automotive surge pushes upward consistently—$~${31.50}B by 2020—because more demand means more battery orders, more learning curves, and faster manufacturing iteration.

Then comes the high-contrast era: 2021–2023. Prices and margins don’t move in a straight line—2021 growth surges (CATL proxy ~${66.30}B; LGES ~${41.00}B; Tesla ~${53.80}B), but the industry’s scale creates pressure that forces cost-down to become non-negotiable. CATL stays near the top through the turbulence (still ~${87.00}B in 2023), while Panasonic’s growth is slower (~${19.60}B by 2023), showing how the market punished lagging execution.

By 2024–2025, the winners look obvious in the chart race: CATL rises again to ~${93.00}B (2024) and ~${105.00}B (2025), while Tesla climbs to ~${112.50}B by 2025.

Now your turn: In an EV battery price crash, is the “winner” the best manufacturer (cells) or the best demand engine (cars)? Drop your pick in the comments—and hit follow for the next timeline battle.
facebook_caption:
The EV battery price crash didn’t just lower sticker prices—it re-ordered the power structure across the supply chain. As manufacturing scaled and learning curves compressed costs, revenue trajectories diverged dramatically among leading cell makers and major EV manufacturers.

In the early period (2005–2010), the industry’s leadership footprint was minimal for several of today’s dominant players. That changed from the mid-2010s onward: CATL’s revenue proxy grows from roughly $8.40B in 2016 to about $23.60B by 2019, reflecting rapid capacity expansion and competitive pricing.

Tesla’s trajectory shows how demand amplified battery scale: from $21.60B in 2016 to $31.50B in 2020, then to approximately $53.80B by 2021. Meanwhile, LG Energy Solution rises into the 2021–2022 surge (~$41.00B to ~$61.00B proxy), then moderates through rebalancing (~$56.00B by 2023).

By 2024–2025, the chart race highlights the surviving cost leaders. CATL reaches about $93.00B (2024) and ~$105.00B (2025), while Tesla climbs to ~$112.50B by 2025. Panasonic’s growth remains steadier and more restrained (~$22.40B by 2025), illustrating how execution speed and scale integration matter when the market forces prices down.

threads_caption:
Okay this timeline is wild. The EV battery price crash didn’t just make cars cheaper—it made the leaderboard turn. 🧯

CATL’s proxy climbs hard after mid-2010s scale (about $8.4B in 2016 → ~$105B by 2025), while Tesla keeps pulling the whole ecosystem upward (from ~$21.6B in 2016 → ~$112.5B by 2025). Meanwhile LGES surges too, then cools during the rebalancing years, and Panasonic stays more restrained.

So—when prices collapse in a tech supply chain, do you think the winners are the cell manufacturers or the companies with the biggest vehicle demand engine? 👇
